questions.q: A retailer feeds a model 50,000 unlabeled customer purchase histories and asks it to find natural groupings. What type of learning is this?
options: Reinforcement learning
Supervised regression
Unsupervised learning
Supervised classification
questions.explain: With no labels supplied, and the goal being to discover structure (like clusters) in the data itself, this is unsupervised learning.

questions.q: In the scikit-learn confusion matrix example, what does it mean that 13 of 16 true versicolor examples were predicted as virginica?
options: The model is perfect on versicolor
The model systematically confuses versicolor for virginica, which a single accuracy number would hide
Virginica and versicolor are the same class
The model never predicts virginica
questions.explain: The confusion matrix shows exactly which classes get mixed up with which — here, most true versicolor examples were misclassified as virginica, a pattern that an overall accuracy score alone would not reveal.

questions.q: What is a "feature vector"?
options: A list of every label in the dataset
One row's full set of feature values
The model's trained parameters
A chart of the model's accuracy over time
questions.explain: A feature vector is simply one example's row of feature values — its full description, minus the label.

questions.q: What happens to a model's internal parameters during inference?
options: They are frozen and unchanged — inference only runs a forward pass
They are reset to random values before every prediction
They are retrained on each new input
They are deleted after each prediction
questions.explain: Inference uses the model's already-trained, fixed parameters to produce an output for a new input; no training or parameter adjustment happens during inference.

questions.q: Why is cross-validation more data-efficient than a single fixed validation split, especially for smaller datasets?
options: It requires collecting additional data beyond what you already have
It never actually evaluates the model
Every sample gets used for both training and evaluation (in different rounds), instead of permanently sacrificing one fixed slice
It eliminates the need for a test set entirely
questions.explain: Rather than permanently setting aside one chunk of data purely for validation, cross-validation rotates the held-out portion across rounds so every sample contributes to both training and evaluation at different points.

questions.q: What does a loss function do?
options: It stores the trained model on disk
It takes a prediction and the true label and returns a single number representing how wrong the prediction was
It splits data into training and test sets
It selects which features to use
questions.explain: A loss function quantifies the gap between a prediction and the true answer as one number, giving the training process something concrete to minimize.

questions.q: What does linear regression predict?
options: A discrete category label
A continuous numeric value, by fitting a straight line (or hyperplane) to the data
A probability distribution over classes only
A cluster assignment
questions.explain: Linear regression fits a straight line (or hyperplane with multiple features) to model the relationship between features and a continuous numeric output.

questions.q: What does a "gini impurity" of 0.0 at a leaf node mean?
options: The node has no training samples at all
Every sample that reaches that leaf belongs to the same class
The tree has not finished training
The feature used at that node is irrelevant
questions.explain: Gini impurity measures how mixed the classes are at a node; 0.0 means the node is perfectly pure — every sample there belongs to a single class.

questions.q: Turning a continuous `days_since_login` value into a binary `is_recently_active` flag (under 30 days) is an example of which pattern?
options: Aggregation
Binning/thresholding
Date decomposition
Ratio/rate normalization
questions.explain: Binning converts a continuous value into a meaningful categorical or binary flag based on a threshold, which is exactly what turning "days since login" into an active/inactive flag does.

questions.q: Why is data leakage considered uniquely dangerous compared to most other ML mistakes?
options: It always crashes the training process immediately, so it's easy to catch
It makes a model look better than it actually is during development, only to fail once the leaked information isn't available in production
It only affects regression models, never classification
It is impossible to detect under any circumstances
questions.explain: Unlike most mistakes, which visibly hurt performance, leakage makes results look artificially strong during development — the danger shows up later, when the model fails in the real world without the leaked information.

questions.q: When might dropping an entire column be more appropriate than imputing it?
options: Whenever a column has even one missing value
When the column is missing in most rows, leaving too little real signal to be worth keeping
Only when the column is categorical
Dropping a column is never appropriate
questions.explain: If a column is missing in the vast majority of rows, there may not be enough real information left in it to justify imputing and keeping it, making dropping the column the more reasonable choice.

questions.q: Why must a fill value (like a column's mean, used to fill missing entries) be learned only from the training split, not the full dataset?
options: Fill values are never allowed in ML pipelines
Computing it from the full dataset (including test rows) leaks information from the test set into training, which is a form of data leakage
The training split always has more rows than the test split
Fill values must always be zero by convention
questions.explain: If a statistic used to clean or fill data is computed using test rows, information from the test set has effectively influenced training — exactly the kind of leakage covered later in this chapter.

questions.q: What happens if you stack two layers with no activation function between them?
options: The network can learn curved decision boundaries
Training becomes impossible to compute
It behaves exactly like ReLU
They algebraically collapse into a single linear function, no matter how many layers you add
questions.explain: The lesson proved this with numbers: h=2x+1 then y=3h-1 equals y=6x+2 at every input — one linear layer in disguise.

questions.q: In the lesson's 4x4 image example, why did the vertical-edge kernel produce different signs (+1 and -1) at different positions?
options: The kernel's weights changed between positions
The image had random noise added
It was a rounding error
The kernel responds to left-right contrast, and the image's contrast pattern flips between the top rows and the bottom rows
questions.explain: The same kernel was applied at each position; the output's sign flipped because the image itself has light-on-left pixels on top and light-on-right pixels on the bottom.

questions.q: What is a 'numerical gradient', and why did the lesson compute one?
options: A gradient computed by nudging a weight slightly and measuring how much the loss changes, used to double-check the chain-rule result
A random number used to initialize weights
The gradient of the activation function alone
A shortcut that replaces backpropagation entirely
questions.explain: The numerical gradient (loss(w+eps) - loss(w-eps)) / (2*eps) matched the chain-rule derivation to four decimal places, confirming the hand-derived gradients were correct.

questions.q: Why does self-attention remove the RNN's long-range bottleneck from lesson 20?
options: It uses a bigger hidden state than RNNs do
It processes tokens in alphabetical order
Every token's score against every other token is a direct calculation, not something relayed through a chain of intermediate steps
It eliminates the need for any numerical computation
questions.explain: Because attention scores are direct dot products between any two tokens, a relationship between distant tokens is exactly as direct as one between adjacent tokens — no information has to survive a long relay.

questions.q: What does 'using a model as-is' mean?
options: Calling a model that someone has already fine-tuned for your exact task, without any further training of your own
Training a model from randomly initialized weights
Deleting the model's tokenizer
Running a model without ever loading its weights
questions.explain: As-is usage means trusting an existing fine-tune — lesson 23's sentiment-analysis pipeline, already fine-tuned on SST-2, is a working example.

questions.q: What is the standard two-line pattern for loading a model from the Hugging Face Hub?
options: AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name) and AutoModel.from_pretrained(name), both given the same model name
A single call to pipeline() with no arguments
Manually downloading a .zip file from the Hub's website
AutoModel.train(name) followed by AutoModel.save(name)
questions.explain: Both the tokenizer and the model are loaded with from_pretrained, keyed off the same model name string.

questions.q: What is the relationship between the Hub and the `transformers` Python library?
options: They are unrelated projects from different companies
transformers replaces the need for the Hub entirely
The Hub only stores transformers' own source code
The Hub is where models and datasets live; transformers is the library that downloads, loads, and runs what the Hub hosts
questions.explain: The Hub hosts the content (models, datasets, Spaces); transformers is the code that reaches into the Hub, downloads a model's files, and runs it.

questions.q: What is transfer learning?
options: Copying a model's files from one computer to another
A method for compressing a model's file size
Training two models at the same time
The principle that knowledge a model learned on one task can be reused to help it on a different task
questions.explain: Transfer learning is the assumption underneath using any pretrained model: that what it learned generalizes beyond the exact task it was originally trained on.

questions.q: What makes `LogisticRegression`'s coefficients useful for understanding this model, beyond just its accuracy?
options: They show exactly how much each feature pushes the prediction toward malignant or benign, letting you sanity-check that the model's reasoning matches real medical intuition
They reveal the exact original training images
They guarantee the model has no errors
They are purely decorative and have no interpretive value
questions.explain: The sign and magnitude of each coefficient show its pull on the prediction. Here, all top coefficients are negative and correspond to features (texture, area, radius, concavity) that pathologists associate with malignancy — a real, if informal, sanity check.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call the matching first-10 predictions "a promising sign, not a final verdict"?
options: Because the model actually got all 10 wrong
Because 10 out of 114 test rows is too small a sample to judge overall performance — the real evaluation covers all 114, which lesson 29 does
Because predictions and true labels are not actually comparable
Because the model hasn't finished training yet at that point
questions.explain: Ten matching predictions out of 114 total test rows is encouraging but not a complete evaluation — lesson 29 scores every one of the 114 predictions, not just the first ten.

questions.q: What does this wrap-up lesson identify as the one throughline connecting all six chapters of AI/ML Foundations?
options: Memorizing the scikit-learn API
Understanding what a model is actually doing, then doing it yourself
Learning as many different algorithms as possible
Focusing exclusively on deep learning
questions.explain: The course moves from conceptual understanding (chapters 1-5) to actually building, training, and evaluating a real model yourself (chapter 6) — that progression is the throughline the recap names.

questions.q: Why is `LogisticRegression` chosen as the capstone's baseline model instead of something more complex?
options: It's the only classifier scikit-learn provides
It guarantees the highest possible accuracy on any dataset
It's a simple, interpretable starting point chosen on purpose — the same role classification was introduced in back in lesson 7
Complex models are against the rules for student capstones
questions.explain: The goal is a correctly built, correctly evaluated baseline, not the fanciest model available — LogisticRegression is picked deliberately as a simple, readable starting point.
